I seen this bird at a wonderful nursery that I like to visit called the North Coast Native Nursery in Petaluma,CA.  Operated by Dave Kaplan it's a wonderful place to find healthy, robust natives of all kinds different applications ( www.northcoastnativenursery.com ). The nursery is situated in the middle of a valley where during the spring the low grasslands become a sort of large vernal marsh. Driving up to the nursery there I found a pair of killdeers in the middle of the dirt road leading up to the greenhouses. Upon closer inspection I found that the pair of mating killdeers had built their nests smack dab in the middle of the dirt road. Eggs well hidden along side the gravel could be barely seen. I was astonished by the incredibly bold birds that would dare such a nest site. The pair would put on a broken wing display to draw the lumbering half ton vehicles up the driveway away from the nest. Each time tire treads coming within inches of crushing the ever fragile eggs. Either these birds were incredibly brave or stupid I could not tell. What I did notice that there was a mass of insects, tadpoles, small frogs and other tasty meals surrounding the nest site. Thankfully enough for the killdeer they are precocial meaning within a few moments from their birth they are walking around. A handy feature when you awake to the world in the middle of a road.

Gray Hawks nest occasionally at Rio Grande Village in Big Bend National Park, Texas. In the summer of 1990 a pair of Gray Hawks fledged two young birds at this location. This is a shot of one of the young birds. The plumage with the broad, pale eye-stripe is distinctive to those who know this species.

An adult Peregrine Falcon spent the winter of 1980-1981 on a bank building in downtown Galveston, Texas. The bird fed mainly on Rock Pigeons (or Rock Doves as they were known in those days). I saw the bird on several occasions during that winter but only took a distant photo in March, shortly before the bird departed for the nesting grounds. The two images show the overall scene through a 300 mm lens and then a cropped shot just of the the falcon. Really makes you appreciate modern digital images when you try to work with 30+ year old slides like this.
Peregrines are regular winter and migrant birds along the Texas coast. This immature Peregrine spent the winter of 1988-1989 at Boca Chica, near where the Rio Grande empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

I was with about 40 other birders on a pelagic trip off of Port Aransas, Texas. We often approached oil rigs out in the Gulf since birds may use them for resting places. On this day we saw about 15 Peregrine Falcons perched on various oil rig platforms. They use these platforms as hunting perches and go after gulls, terns, or other species. Image 1 shows one of the birds perched on a platform (appears to be a juvenile bird), while image 2 shows three birds, although they are hard to make out. One is perched above the "N" on the white sign while two are near the right edge of the structure. I have seen as many as 6 Peregrines perched on one platform.

This stunning rarity was the 1st Texas record of Blue-footed Booby. The bird was present at this large fresh-water lake for more than a year, from June 1993 to 6 October 1994. Interestingly, two other Blue-footed Boobies showed up in the southwestern U.S. at about the same time, one in Nevada and one in California. I saw this bird on at least a dozen occasions during the above time period. This shot was taken 22 April 1994. After leaving the Granite Shoals location on Lake L.B.J., the bird moved down the Colorado River and was found on Lake Bastrop, s.e. of Austin, where it stayed 6 months, then disappeared. Black-capped Chickadees are found in Alaska, Canada, and The Northern United States.  The birds irregularly migrate toward the south during the winter, and they build their nests in hollowed trees and stumps.  Chickadees eat mainly insects and spiders, but also eat berries, seeds, and suet.  Chickadees are hunted by hawks, owls, Raccoons, and some squirrels.  A black-capped Chickadees are important to an ecosystem because they help control the insect population and help disperse seeds.  They are also a major food source for many predators too.

On 9 April, 2009, on a wet stormy day in a clearing low down in Hinewai Reserve, tui were released back onto Banks Peninsula. It is hoped that these birds will found a breeding population on Banks Peninsula, the first since at least the 1980s. In the previous week, 30 tui had been caught on Maud Island in the Marlborough Sounds, a predator-free reserve managed by the Department of Conservation. The captured tui, a mixture of male and female adults and juveniles, were placed in cardboard cat boxes, two to a box, and flown by helicopter directly to Hinewai Reserve. If these 30 birds stick around, they will be joined by a further 50 birds from Maud Island next year. In this photo, a tui is released by Wayne Beggs, from the Department of Conservation, and John Tom, a retired vet from nearby Akaroa. A friend of mine had set his backpack down on the beach while he went swimming in the ocean. Those of us still on the beach saw a huge baboon walking towards us (http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/1198219). We all took a few steps back, but the monkey went straight for the backpack and started rustling through its contents. One of my professors through his flip-flops at it, but the baboon did not leave. Eventually, it dragged the pack up to the top of the sand dune. None of us were sure what to do to recover the bag. Suddenly, out of nowhere, an ostrich came running straight at the baboon. The baboon took off running down the beach, and the ostrich simply turned around and walked away.

This Pyrrhuloxia, also known as a Desert Cardinal, was seen amongst 6 other birds (at least one of which was a different species, the Chipping Sparrow) in an arroyo.  It landed in a dry bush after being scared up by our ATV.  It can be identified by its thick and stubby yellow bill, which is curved, grey head, back and upperparts, dark grey wings with red edge, red tail feathers, red face, and very obvious red-tipped grey crest on top of the head.  This individual was likely female, as she lacked the red crest (only had a small red tip to the crest), and had no red mottling on the chest.  The Pyrrhuloxia eats flower spikes, various fruits, berries, seeds, insects or larvae.  It was a sunny day, approximately 55 degrees Fahrenheit, and quite windy

Observed walking in the water in a small pond located in the center of the University of Texas Marine Science Campus. The bird was solitary, not seen interacting with any other individuals of the same or different species. The pond was located directly next to a paved road and within 5-10m of 2-3 buildings. The bird was often seen walking in the shallow (5-10 cm) water along the edge of the pond, often in the tall (1-1.5m) grasses. Occasionally when walking along the road, the bird would either quickly walk north/northwest in the water, away from us, or would fly to the northwest end of the pond. The bird, while sometime skittish, seemed somewhat desensitized to the presence of humans. It was often seen in the morning and at dusk. heron was identifiable by its long legs, long blue-grey neck, blue-grey body, long, dagger-like bill, and white head with black feathers forming a line going from the eye to the back of the head. Conditions at the time of this observation were 54F and overcast with 11.5 mph ENE winds.

The great egret -Ardea alba-, also known as the common egret, large egret or -in the Old World- great white heron,is a large, widely distributed egret. Distributed across most of the tropical and warmer temperate regions of the world. The great egret is a large heron with all-white plumage. Standing up to 1 m tall, this species can measure 80 to 104 cm -31 to 41 in-, Apart from size, the great egret can be distinguished from other white egrets by its yellow bill and black legs and feet, though the bill may become darker and the lower legs lighter in the breeding season. In breeding plumage, delicate ornamental feathers are borne on the back. Males and females are identical in appearance. It has a slow flight, with its neck retracted. The great egret is not normally a vocal bird; it gives a low hoarse croak when disturbed, and at breeding colonies, it often gives a loud croaking cuk cuk cuk and higher-pitched squawks.

28 December 2014: Observed a Curve-billed Thrasher (Toxostoma curvirostre) resting atop large thorny brush in the chaparral off to the side of a hiking trail at the Amistad National Recreation Area (ANRA) which is administered by the US National Parks Service (USNPS). The location is situated a few miles to the north of the twin cities of Del Río, Texas and Ciudad Acuña, Coahuila.

According to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s All About Birds Web site, the Curve-billed Thrasher does not migrate but rather is a bird found in the greater Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts on both sides of the US-Mexico border—Mexico’s north and the US Southwest. It ranges into New Mexico and some southern parts of Arizona, as well as small areas of the most northwestern corner of Oklahoma and the most southeastern corner of Colorado.  Essentially, the whole of the Río Bravo/Río Grande basin is one where this large songbird may be found as its range extends along the entire course of the river down into the southernmost parts of Texas in what Tejanos call El Valle, also known as the Río Grande Valley. The Curve-billed Thrasher is found in most of Mexico as to its southern range except the Baja California peninsula (to the west) and the most southeastern states. This is a bird that’s clearly identified with the Río Grande/Río Bravo Basin (and therein the peoples of the states mentioned) to its northeast and with the deserts of the Mexican far north (Sonora, Chihuahua, Coahuila, Nuevo León, and Tamaulipas, etc.).  But it is one that is also familiar to Mexicans who live in its central, western and southwestern Pacific states as well as its southcentral states though it might be scarce or less common on the Gulf of Mexico’s coastal states south beyond Tamaulipas.

As to its US southwestern range, All About Birds provides this very short thumbnail sketch: “A common bird of the arid Southwest, the Curve-billed Thrasher occurs in a range of habitats. Perhaps because of its broader tolerances, it is the most widespread of the western thrashers.” It has a wingspan nearly 14 inches long and its length nearly reaches 11inches.

23 July 2015: Observed a single Yellow-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus americanus) perched up a tree branch at Elm Fork Park, Greenbelt Corridor, Lake Ray Roberts/Lake Lewisville State Park, Access Area FM 455, Denton County, Texas (between Pilot Point and Sanger, Texas).

This was my first observation in the wild of this bird and the first time I've observed the Yellow-billed Cuckoo at Elm Fork Park. The bird was perched a distance away which explains the digital image. And it only gave me opportunity to take but two digital frames before flying off thus living up to its reported secretive nature. Among the insects they prefer to eat are cicadas and there were plenty of cicadas at Elm Fork Park loudly announcing their presence. Hundreds of dragonflies were flying as well in the area where this bird was sighted. 

Mark Lockwood of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department prepared a "Birds of Ray Roberts Lake State Park: A Field Checklist" (January 2010) that's available online here: https://tpwd.texas.gov/publications/pwdpubs/media/pwd_bk_p4503_0137u.pdf . Lockwood determined that the Yellow-billed Cuckoo is "common" at this site during spring, summer and fall.

The Yellow-billed Cuckoo is a true migrant and bird of the Americas, an American bird writ large, since it occurs from the most southeastern corner of Canada's provinces and on into or across the eastern half of the United States (with reduced presence in specific sites of various states in the US West). The bird's extensive wintering migration ranges widely continuing into Mexico through Texas primarily (where this bird is presumably found throughout the entire state) and Central and South America as far as the northern reaches of Argentina. The only country in South America where the Yellow-billed Cuckoo reportedly does not fly is Chile. The Caribbean island nations are also home for the Yellow-billed Cuckoo. This bird is native to most countries in the Western Hemisphere. In Texas, it is generally present from April to October, though it is considered to be far less common west of Central Texas.

In the United States its presence in the West and to a lesser but notable extent in the East has been declining for decades. During the first half of the 20th century the Yellow-billed Cuckoo disappeared entirely from the Pacific Northwest of the United States and Canada's far Southwest (British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon).

Elm Fork Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD).

Sources: All About Birds - Cornell Lab of Ornithology, BirdLife International, Texas Breeding Bird Atlas, and Wikipedia.

24 April 2015: Observed an Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe) catch a green caterpillar and prepare to ingest it. Eastern Phoebes nest and raise their broods in the Avondale Park and Cooper Creek areas of Denton, Texas. Since Eastern Phoebes raise from 1-2 broods per year, the green caterpillar in the beak of this adult bird may have meant that their first brood was already being raised nearby.

Eastern Phoebes are a North American species that is native to Canada, United States and Mexico, according to the range map provided by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's All About Birds online encyclopedia on the birds of North America. Eastern Phoebes live year-round in some parts of North and East Texas and other areas of the South and Southeast of the US. It also migrates to large areas of the Canadian north and winters in half or more of Mexico's eastern and central states.

The particular subject in this digital image is a year-round resident of Avondale Park and Cooper Creek.

Apparently, the southern range of the Eastern Phoebe does not extend into the Caribbean or past Mexico into Central and South America.

4 January 2015: Observed and photographed this tiny and quick, energetic bird in the thick of winter with the temps down in the low thirties at the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC) in Denton, Texas near the confluence of Clear Creek and the Elm Fork Trinity River. This bird is a migratory bird to the North Texas region, it is not a year-round resident. The City of Denton administers the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC).

All About Birds (Cornell Lab of Ornithology) had this to say in their thumbnail sketch of this wren: "Small in stature and incomparably energetic in voice, the Winter Wren inhabits moist forests and other habitats across much of eastern North America. They were formerly considered one species that occupied northern forests across the globe. But in 2010, on the basis of vocalizations and genetics, they were split into three species, including the Pacific Wren of western North America and the Eurasian Wren in the Old World."

During the non-breeding winter season this bird ranges over the central and eastern half of Texas and across most of the eastern half of the United States. It breeds in spring and summer in the northern reaches of the United States particularly in the northernmost areas of North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan east to all of New England and on into Canada's eastern, midwestern and northwestern provinces to some extent as well.  

New Englanders and Canadians know this tiny songbird as a spring to early fall resident.  Its range does not extend past its Texas range which is the southernmost extent of the Winter Wren's migration.  Mexico does not experience the Winter Wren's migration except perhaps as a vagrant or accidental instance. This is an authentic North American songbird.

Turkey Vulture over the Elm Fork Trinity River

1 July 2015: Observed a single Turkey Vulture (Cathartes aura) perched atop a dead tree overlooking the Elm Fork Trinity River downstream a mile from the Lake Ray Roberts dam's spillway at Elm Fork Park, Denton County, Texas (between Pilot Point and Sanger). As we began to photograph the Turkey Vulture it allowed sufficient time to obtain excellent digital images and then eventually after a good long while decided it was time to take to the air and it is these final digital images that we present here (in the four images above).

The Turkey Vulture is arguably the most widespread bird of its kind in the Americas - of the entire Western Hemisphere (see All About Birds' range map, Cornell Lab of Ornithology). Everyone and anyone in the Western Hemisphere who has ever looked up at the sky and wondered in awe or otherwise what those soaring black birds were way up on high will know they have seen a Turkey Vulture. Known for how it is that they make flight look so effortless once they're in actual flight, Turkey Vultures have an unrivaled extensive range that encompasses the southernmost reaches of Canada's southern provinces from the Pacific to the Atlantic. From there the entirety of the United States, Mexico, Central America, Caribbean and South America constitute the Turkey Vulture's domain. Widespread and abundant wherever they occur, Turkey Vultures are iconic big birds embedded in folklore, history and culture. Wherever their presence has been known they have imprinted themselves on the peoples and societies that have experienced them.

Turkey Vultures perform invaluable service to societies, peoples and wildlife everywhere in that they identify and consume dead carcasses. According to the thumbnail sketch provided by All About Birds, they "ride thermals in the sky and use their keen sense of smell to find fresh carcasses. They are a consummate scavenger, cleaning up the countryside one bite of their sharply hooked bill at a time, and never mussing a feather on their bald heads."

A Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources website had this to say about the Turkey Vulture: "Biologists once thought that the turkey vulture was a bird of prey and a raptor like hawks, owls, and eagles. But, in 1994, scientists used DNA tests and found that they belonged in the stork family. This is where they are classified today." See: http://dnr.wi.gov/org/caer/ce/eek/critter/bird/turkeyvulture.htm

For longer than human beings have resided in what we now know as the Western Hemisphere, Turkey Vultures have performed their timeless watch high above the land making sure all things get noticed and given their proper attention.

True Americans long before the continents of the Western Hemisphere were thus named, Turkey Vultures are timeless reminders of a wildness that precedes us.

Elm Fork Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD).

This is the thumbnail sketch presented by the online North American birds encyclopedia hosted by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds, on the Ruby-throated Hummingbird: "A flash of green and red, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird is eastern North America’s sole breeding hummingbird. These brilliant, tiny, precision-flying creatures glitter like jewels in the full sun, then vanish with a zip toward the next nectar source. Feeders and flower gardens are great ways to attract these birds, and some people turn their yards into buzzing clouds of hummingbirds each summer. Enjoy them while they’re around; by early fall they’re bound for Central America, with many crossing the Gulf of Mexico in a single flight."

Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are an authentic North American bird. In their southernmost range they winter along the coastal reaches of Mexico's southwestern Pacific states and the southern and southeastern states that border on the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic closest to Central America whence their farthest wintering grounds are to be found. While most of Central America is home to this native hummer, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird's range does not extend beyond the southern countries of Central America into the South American continent.

To the north, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird's range extends as far north as Canada's midwestern and eastern provinces especially those southern areas therein closest to the border with the United States. The entire eastern half of the United States is home to this native hummer including Texas that provides a land bridge in this tiny bird's annual migration north and south. Only the most western areas of West Texas and the Panhandle are excluded from the Ruby-thorated Hummingbird's range. Equally, Mexico's most northwestern states starting with Chihuahua going west including Sonora, and the two Baja Califronias, Norte and Sur, are outside the range of this busy annual flyer. This jewel of the Western Hemisphere is a North American bird that's a wonder to behold.

Bald Eagle  (Haliaeetus leucocephalus)

31 October 2014: Observed a single Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) flying high over the Lake Lewisville dam catching the uplifting wind currents coming off of the large earthen dam and the nearby large body of water. Lake Lewisville’s surface area measures 29,592 acres. We heard said that a lone eagle had been coming to winter in LLELA for the past few years and presumably this is that single eagle that’s been making its appearance at LLELA in the recent past.  The attraction for this Bald Eagle appears to be the abundant fish available in Lake Lewisville and the Elm Fork Trinity River. LLELA is administered jointly by the US Corps of Engineers, the City of Lewisville, Texas, the Lewisville Independent School District, and the University of North Texas.

This is the thumbnail sketch offered by All About Birds on the Bald Eagle: “The Bald Eagle has been the national emblem of the United States since 1782 and a spiritual symbol for native people for far longer than that. These regal birds aren’t really bald, but their white-feathered heads gleam in contrast to their chocolate-brown body and wings. Look for them soaring in solitude, chasing other birds for their food, or gathering by the hundreds in winter. Once endangered by hunting and pesticides, Bald Eagles have flourished under protection.” 

Terry Sohl’s excellent range map for the Bald Eagle provided by NatureServe depicts the extent of the Bald Eagle’s range. Clearly, the Bald Eagle is a North American bird, a big bird, a raptor. It has permanent residence in scattered continental locations from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Evidently most but not all of the locations where the Bald Eagle resides permanently tend to be areas within the United States including Alaska. To be more precise, the Bald Eagle takes permanent residence along the Pacific coastline mountainous range from Alaska through Canada and on into the Pacific Northwest up to just shy of the state line in northern California. But California has a large mountainous area in its northernmost region that is home to a permanent population of Bald Eagles, removed from the coast proper. On the East Coast, the Bald Eagle is a permanent resident of practically the entire state of Florida all the way up the Atlantic coastline to southern New Jersey. A few states in the continental United States constitute a permanent home to the Bald Eagle in the entirety of their territory. These states include Florida, Idaho and Delaware, and most of Maryland and Montana are also a permanent range for the Bald Eagle but not quite so. The habitat favored by the Bald Eagle includes mountainous areas when such habitat is removed from the ocean coastlines or if not the coastlines proper. Other states that have permanent range for the Bald Eagle include Arizona, Colorado and Wyoming. On the East Coast, besides those states already mentioned, states that support a coastal community of Bald Eagles on a permanent basis include Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia and the far southeastern corner of Pennsylvania closest to the Atlantic coast. All of the US states in the Midwest and West of the country provide non-breeding residence part of the year for the Bald Eagle or a combination of both permanent and non-permanent habitat. Sohl’s range map has the Bald Eagle generally avoiding the Appalachian Mountains on the East of the country. And the Bald Eagle is particular about where it flies to breed and the larger brunt of that region tends to be located in Canada from coast to coast—West to East and vice versa. The area around the Great Lakes is also prime breeding range for this raptor and thus several US states in that area including (west to east) Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Maine in their northernmost areas are home to breeding populations of Bald Eagles.

The Bald Eagle ranges south into Mexico during the non-breeding season and makes a home annually in this manner in several mostly northern Mexican states including (west to east) Baja California Norte, Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua, Durango, Coahuila, Tamaulipas and Veracruz. In Mexico the Bald Eagle repeats its range pattern found to the north of the continent in that it flies or may be found on either coast and favors mountainous range removed from the coastlines as well. But beyond these Mexican states its range does not extend farther south. It is mostly a bird that favors the northern continental latitudes; it favors high elevations, and favors ocean coastline habitats.

The Bald Eagle is a resident of North America and a magnificent sight to see in the wild. It is and has been a longtime authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Barred Owl (Strix varia)

11 August 2015: Walked the Onion Creek Trail alongside Onion Creek at the McKinney Falls State Park which is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) and came upon a Barred Owl (Strix varia). We were only able to get one digital pic before the owl flew off. It had been standing atop the highest reaches of the giant cypresses that are found on the banks of Onion Creek. We were too far and our equipment too limited to be able to obtain a better image but still we believe the particular species is identifiable from the evidence presented. We hope there will be better opportunities to photograph this and other owls in future. Barred Owl is unquestionably an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Es una ave acuática del orden Ciconiiformes de la familia Ardeidae . Se alimentan de peces, ranas e insectos principalmente en aguas poco profundas.
Mide 66 cm. y pesa 350 grs. Es delgado, con el pico largo y el cuello muy alargado. En los adultos la cabeza, cuello y la región superior son principalmente de color gris plomizo. La raya a lo largo de la parte anterior del cuello es castaña y blanca. El cuello y el pecho son más purpúreos, con rayas castañas, y el abdomen y el forro de las alas son blancos. La piel de la cara es amarillo naranja con una mancha fusca en el área loreal. El iris es amarillo anteado, el pico es de color cuerno y se torna fusco hacia el culmen, y las patas son amarillas. Durante la época reproductiva las plumas son blancuzcas alargadas en la parte posterior del cuello y anteadas en la espalda. Los ejemplares inmaduros presentan la cabeza, manto y el cuello de color gris parduzco; el resto es parecido al adulto, aunque sin las plumas alargadas. Los individuos juveniles exhiben un patrón similar al de los adultos, pero con el cuello café rojizo opaco y el manto café oliva en vez de gris.

Harris's Sparrow (Zonotrichia querula)

6 December 2014: A whole host of sparrows settle into the North Texas region as they migrate in retreat from the northern winter and one of the places they frequent is the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC), in Denton, Texas which is the county seat of the similarly named Denton County. The CCNHC is a nature preserve of 2,000 acres approximately and it is bordered by the Clear Creek and the Elm Fork Trinity River and the confluence of these two bodies of water occurs at the juncture called The Confluence within the boundaries of this nature preserve.And the Harris's Sparrow (Zonotrichia querula) is one of these migrating sparrows that arrives in the North Texas area during the mid to late fall of the year and leaves to return northward sometime in early spring. It is a particular migratory pattern. We photographed several separate Harris's Sparrows on this day at the CCNHC. We present a digital image of one of these sparrows in this observation. The CCNHC is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Harris's Sparrow's range is a central one up and down the heart of North America. It summers and breeds in the highest latitudes nearly of Canada's central provinces up close to the Arctic Sea and Hudson Bay and migrates through Canada's central southern provinces and the midwestern states of the United States south and north according to the season but winters in the southcentral states of the Midwest through Texas. Harris's Sparrow apparently does not travel much into Mexico and its southernmost range is found in South Texas up to the Río Bravo and the Gulf of Mexico. Because it is a North American flier of the central continental flyway Harris's Sparrow is most definitely an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Sources: 

"Harris's Sparrow," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, description and range map, accessed 9.25.15, http://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Harriss_Sparrow/id

I'm going back to some of my earliest wildlife images. These are scans from old prints and slides.  This will rank as the worst image I will ever upload to iNat--really quite unidentifiable from the photo--but it was a significant record at the time...so here it is.

Mark Lockwood had discovered a Greater Pewee in a city park S of Big Spring, TX, on Oct. 22, 1984, which was the first well-documented report from Texas for the species (TBRC 1985-3; TPRF 329) (Amer. Birds 39:74).  I finally made it up to Big Spring to search for the bird on Nov. 17.  I found the bird within 5 minutes as it gave "pip-pip" calls from tree tops and a power line.  It sang its characteristic "Jose Maria" song once.  The day was heavily overcast, dark, and drizzly and this was the only image I obtained of the bird.  It was shot backlit against the heavy clouds in mid-afternoon.  This turned out to be the last date it was seen.

Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus)

23 October 2015: In visiting Tualatin River National Wildlife Refuge for the first time we came upon one of three different chickadees that reside in the state of Oregon, the Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus). And we were able to observe and photograph it for the first time. The particular individual in our photographs was busy feeding on the tips of the leaves of the Oregon White Oak that did not make it to maturity before the onset of fall and the coming winter. Black-capped Chickadee is a non-migrating bird that's found year-round in the Pacific Northwest and across most of the continental United States from the West to East Coast and the same is true for Canada where all except its most northern areas are home to this small songbird. Its range extends into central and southwestern Alaska and constitutes its most northern and western range as well. Black-capped Chickadee's range does not extend for the most part into the US Southwest and Southeast. Tualatin River National Wildlife Refuge is administered by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, US Department of the Interior and the many volunteers whose generosity makes possible its daily operation. Because of its expansive range in North America, Black-capped Chickadee is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Sources: 

"Birds: Chickadees and Nuthatches," Oregon Wildlife Species, Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, description, photograph, comparison with other similar birds in the state, accessed 11.1.15, http://www.dfw.state.or.us/species/birds/chickadees_nuthatches.asp

"Black-capped Chickadee," All About Birds, Cornell University Lab of Ornithology, range map, description, songs, photographs, accessed 11.1.15, http://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/black-capped_chickadee/lifehistory

Osprey (Pandion haliaetus)

31 October 2014: On a visit to the Lewisville Lake Environmental Learning Area (LLELA) in Lewisville, Texas we hiked the Redbud Trail and encountered a pair of Ospreys (Pandion haliaetus) flying overhead and fishing in the adjacent Elm Fork Trinity River as it flows south toward Dallas and its own eventual joining with the Trinity River. One of them flew close enough to us and thence overhead that we were able to take a few pics of its having just caught a large fish in the Elm Fork Trinity River. This observation shares some of these pics. According to the LLELA Bird Checklist available online Osprey is either rare or uncommon Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter at this site with its being rare in particular during the summertime. All About Birds has this to say about Osprey: “Unique among North American raptors for its diet of live fish and ability to dive into water to catch them, Ospreys are common sights soaring over shorelines, patrolling waterways, and standing on their huge stick nests, white heads gleaming. These large, rangy hawks do well around humans and have rebounded in numbers following the ban on the pesticide DDT. Hunting Ospreys are a picture of concentration, diving with feet outstretched and yellow eyes sighting straight along their talons.” Meanwhile, the folks over at Audubon have this to say in their thumbnail sketch of Osprey at their online site: “A very distinctive fish-hawk, formerly classified with other hawks but now placed in a separate family of its own. Along coastlines, lakes, and rivers almost worldwide, the Osprey is often seen flying over the water, hovering, and then plunging feet-first to catch fish in its talons. After a successful strike, the bird rises heavily from the water and flies away, carrying the fish head-forward with its feet. Bald Eagles sometimes chase Ospreys and force them to drop their catch. In many regions, landowners put up poles near the water to attract nesting Ospreys.” Ospreys fly therefore globally and because of this they are most certainly authentic residents of the Western Hemisphere and equally so of planet Earth. In the Western Hemisphere Osprey is known from north to south as it winters in South America and covers much of the southern continent’s territory, while it is known as a migrant fish-hawk throughout the Americas to the north and it claims coastlines including in the Caribbean either as a permanent home or as breeding grounds or simply as a temporary stop on its migration elsewhere. Its breeding grounds in the main though are located in the northern latitudes from Alaska on south and east across the vast expanse of the Canadian plains, forests, and mountains from the Pacific to the Atlantic. Some areas in the US West, Pacific Northwest, and the Great Lakes also serve as breeding ground for Osprey and the whole of the Baja California Peninsula is a permanent home for Osprey as is also the Florida Peninsula. The Gulf of Mexico’s coastline in Mexico and the United States provides wintering ground for Osprey, and generally it claims such spaces in the Americas north and south. At Lake Lewisville and LLELA generally Osprey finds plenty of fish to eat at both the Elm Fork Trinity River and Lake Lewisville proper. LLELA is jointly administered by a consortium that includes the US Army Corps of Engineers, the City of Lewisville, Texas, the Lewisville Independent School District, and the University of North Texas.

Winter Wren (Troglodytes hiemalis)

19 December 2015: In the course of completing the final Bird Walk of the year at the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC) in Denton, Texas, we came upon this tiny representative of the Winter Wren (Troglodytes hiemalis) on the Wetlands Trails (otherwise marked Duck Trail on the Google map that accompanies this observation). The Winter Wren is an entirely North American species as per the thumbnail sketch found on All About Birds: "Small in stature and incomparably energetic in voice, the Winter Wren inhabits moist forests and other habitats across much of eastern North America. They were formerly considered one species that occupied northern forests across the globe. But in 2010, on the basis of vocalizations and genetics, they were split into three species, including the Pacific Wren of western North America and the Eurasian Wren in the Old World." Because of its North American presence in Canada and United States, Winter Wren is an incontrovertibly authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The CCNHC is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Source: "Winter Wren," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, photographs, range map, description, resource links, accessed 12.20.15, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Winter_Wren/id

Broad-winged Hawk (Buteo platypterus)

23 June 2014: Flying high over the sky of Avondale Park in circular motion and perhaps foraging the area on its way north to the eastern half of the United States and central and southeastern Canada from its wintering grounds in Central America and South America to begin to take up anew its vast breeding range, we observed a single Broad-tailed Hawk (Buteo platypterus). The images posted in this observation are the only ones we took of this hawk. It is not one we have seen again since during the coming and going of seasons. Broad-tailed Hawk is a migratory bird through this area though its breeding range begins not far to the north and east of our region in the North Texas metropolitan area. Because of its extensive range that it covers between North and South America and points and places in between, Broad-tailed Hawk is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon)

15 March 2015: We observed this male Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) land atop a still leafless Mesquite tree next to The Pond alongside the Wetlands Trail (aka Duck Trail on our Google map on iNat) toward the official end of winter. We were a bit distant from its perch and the images presented in this observation reflect that plus the sky was intermittently cloudy throughout our time at the site. Belted Kingfisher is permanently found throughout most of the continental United States and it winters in that portion of the nation where it doesn't otherwise reside on a permanent basis. In the most northern parts of the Upper Midwest states like Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan, east to the Great Lakes, Belted Kingfisher claims a breeding territory. And in Canada its presence is almost exclusively that of a breeding range as with so many other species of North American birds and this vast breeding range extends from the Atlantic Coast on the east thence westward to the Pacific Ocean and north and west to cover almost all of the state of Alaska at its most northern range. Interestingly, Belted Kingfisher also claims a permanent range all along the Pacific Coast of Canada northward and west through Alaska to the Aleutian Islands. Beginning in South Texas thence west all the way to southern California (passing through New Mexico and Arizona) south through Mexico, the Carribbean, Central America, and ending up in the northern fringes of the South American continent lies the seemingly limitless wintering range of Belted Kingfisher which is both a wintering bird, a migratory one, and a permanent resident as well. Again, most of its permanent range is located in the United States, in Canada to some extent up its Pacific Coast to Alaska, and in Alaska proper. In South America, Belted Kingfisher winters along the Atlantic Ocean coastal areas of Colombia, Venezuela, and Guyana. It is here that it reaches the southern extent of its transcontinental range in the Western Hemisphere, and because it does Belted Kingfisher is the inimitable authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The 2,900-acre CCNHC is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Northern Flicker (Colaptes auratus)

1 January 2016: We had the opportunity to visit the Hagerman National Wildlife Refuge (HNWR) in Sherman, Texas, on the first day of the new year. It was a partly cloudy and wintry day. Though entrance to the intersection of Bennett Lane and Wildlife Road was possible one could not go much farther as most roads were closed beyond this entry point to the refuge due to extensive flooding at the site. The waters of Lake Texoma were swollen and the HNWR was effectively closed except for access to the point that we and others at the site were able to reach. But in walking the limited perimeter of what was possible at the site we were able to photograph some birds and could  hear others in the distance as they freely exchanged and interacted verbally and loudly with one another. These others were bigger birds, hawks, crows, gulls, and ducks. The Northern Flicker (Colaptes auratus) in our observation allowed us to get close within limits and among the results is the image presented. Northern Flicker is a North American woodpecker and is nearly present on a permanent basis throughout all of the continental United States except for areas of southern California and the western half of Texas where it is a wintering migrant, and another section of southern Arizona where it is apparently absent entirely, at least according to the range map at All About Birds. Its permanent range extends into the southern reaches of Canada bordering with the United States especially its southwestern region and up along the Pacific coastline to just shy of Alaska's border with Canada. And similarly, a section of southeastern Canada has the permanent presence of Northern Flicker. Most of Alaska though provides a breeding range for Northern Flicker as does the rest of Canada from Alaska east across the vast continental mass that is Canada. Also, Northern Flicker makes a permanent home in the Caribbean and most certainly in Cuba, the largest of the Caribbean Island nations. So does Mexico as there's a long territory extending from the area where New Mexico and Arizona meet south along along the western Sierra Madre and similarly along the eastern Sierra Madre range south into central Mexico and its Pacific Southwest thence this range intermittently jumps into Central America as far south as an area of northern Nicaragua where the permanent range of Northern Flicker meets its most southern extent. Beyond this point its presence does not extend into the southern areas of Central America or into the South American continent. Because of its extensive North American presence, Northern Flicker is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The HNWR is administered by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, U.S. Department of the Interior.

Franklin’s Gull (Larus pipixcan)

3 May 2015: Franklin’s Gull (Larus pipixcan) is an entirely migratory aquatic bird of the Western Hemisphere per the range maps provided online (see Sources section below). Franklin’s Gull shares migratory, wintering, and breeding ranges along a north-south axis from the south-central provinces of Canada at its greatest point north to nearly the southern tip of Chile on that nation’s south Atlantic coastline, where it winters and represents this species’ most southern range. Franklin’s Gull’s breeding range may be found also in some of the Upper Midwest states of the United States including Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and the northwest corner of Minnesota. In addition, there are some discontinuous or  intermittent breeding ranges in the western half of the United States favored by this gull and these occur in Idaho, Nevada, Utah (in the vicinity of the Great Salt Lake), Wyoming, and Montana, where it already shares a significant space as breeding range. The rest of its flight and residence in the United States is strictly migratory and it occurs down through the central areas of the nation and Mexico’s territory as well avoiding the northwestern corner of the country and its Baja California Peninsula entirely except as vagrants. This flight continues into Central America and Franklin’s Gull favors the Pacific coastline to reach its ultimate wintering range along the entire length almost of the South American continent from Ecuador, then Peru and ultimately the long storied coastline of Chile. We would not be surprised if the great Chilean poet Pablo Neruda studied the habits of Franklin’s Gull at one time or another on his beloved Isla Negra as he was fond of the ocean and its creatures given the geography of his nation and experience of its peoples. There were several Franklin’s Gulls high above Lewisville Lake and the Lake Lewisville Environmental Learning Area (LLELA) on the day we made this observation and we were able to hone in with our camera on one of these which is represented in our images. The characteristic markings of this gull in flight distinguish it from its most closely looking cousin while in flight, Laughing Gull. The whole of Texas is in the path of its migratory flight north and south and thus Franklin’s Gull appears twice annually in the North Texas region when it comes and goes on its ages old migratory flight. Because of its amazing longitudinal flight in North and South America, Franklin’s Gull is authentically and originally a resident of the Western Hemisphere. LLELA is administered jointly in partnership by the US Army Corps of Engineers, the City of Lewisville, Texas, the Lewisville Independent School District, and the University of North Texas.

Green-winged Teal (Anas crecca)

(Anas crecca carolinensis)

7 March 2015: The ever-changing Wetlands Lake at the Clear Creek Natural Heritage Center (CCNHC) in Denton, Texas, offered up this observation during the late winter season. The digital images presented in this observation are of four male Green-winged Teals (Anas crecca) and one female accompanied on their takeoff (sensing our approach) from the lake’s surface by a lone male Blue-winged Teal. Green-winged Teal is a duck species of North America but one that also occurs in Eurasia. The farthest southern extent of their wintering range occurs in southern Mexico and in the Caribbean where it resides during its winter migration in Cuba and other Island nations. The NatureServe range map also appears to indicate that Green-winged Teal occurs as a vagrant on both the Pacific and Atlantic Coasts of several Central American nations. And on the northern edge of South America on the Atlantic Coast of Venezuela there appears to be a small, even tiny, permanent range for Green-winged Teal. If so, this Venezuelan permanent range would constitute its most southern range in the hemisphere. Nearly all of Mexico except for the region associated with the Yucatan Peninsula provides a wintering range for Green-winged Teal, thus it is a duck that people in Mexico observe annually and indicates the flexible capacity to adapt to different altitudes and environments of this species. All the southern half of the United States provides wintering range as well and its single largest permanent range occurs in several US West states including Washington, Oregon, Montana, Idaho, North Dakota, South Dakota, Colorado, Nevada, California and Arizona. This range is spread far apart and is intermittent at points. Where Green-winged Teal does not winter within the United States, it migrates and also claims a breeding range in the region associated with the Great Lakes states of the Upper Midwest and the Northeast and thence all of Canada to the north and Alaska to the northwest and north comprise breeding range for Green-winged Teal. Indeed the northern regions of Alaska and its Arctic Ocean constitute the farthest northern range for Green-winged Teal. Green-winged Teal occurs in the Western Hemisphere (Anas crecca carolinensis) and in Eurasia (Anas crecca crecca). Because of its extensive flight north and south throughout the Americas, Green-winged Teal is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. And indeed this is a species that flies over large parts of the world. The CCNHC is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe)

31 October 2014: Next to the bank of the Elm Fork Trinity River we observed an Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe) at the Lewisville Lake Environmental Learning Area (LLELA) in Lewisville, Texas. We're fortunate in the North Texas region to have this flycatcher and songbird as a permanent resident. Eastern Phoebe is strictly a North American bird with its breeding, wintering, migratory and permanent ranges located in Canada, United States and Mexico. It occurs in the Caribbean only as a vagrant, while its large wintering range in Mexico encompasses nearly the entire eastern half of the nation extending down the Gulf of Mexico coastline nearly to where the state of Veracruz meets with the state of Tabasco. Eastern Phoebe's range does not extend into the Yucatan Peninsula or into Central America. Eastern Phoebe does not occur in the westernmost areas of Mexico or the United States. In these latter regions instead its close cousin the Black Phoebe takes up its own range to fill in where its kin leaves off. Because of its extensive North American range, Eastern Phoebe is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. LLELA is administered by a joint partnership consisting of the US Army Corps of Engineers, the City of Lewisville, Texas, the Lewisville Independent School District, and the University of North Texas.

The statue it is perched on is near my feeders so many birds land on it and this bird was not significantly larger than any of the Western Scrub-Jays that also use it. Additionally, one of the outer tail feathers appears separated from the rest, yet is the same length as the central feathers.

Canvasback (Aythya valisineria) - male

7 February 2016: Visited South Lakes Park and observed a single male Canvasback (Aythya valisineria) among the Lesser Scaups, Mallards, Pied-billed Grebes, Double-crested Cormorants, and Ring-billed Gulls, among others present at the site. We'd not photographed the Canvasback previously so this is our initial entry for Canvasback. We noticed (see Image 2) that this particular Canvasback had a clear-colored fishing line caught in one of its feet and dragging behind the end of the fishing line (noticeable when it was in flight) was a long vine from some sort of water plant. This is a reminder to those who fish to pick up all you carry into the site where you fish as fishing line can easily become a problem in the environment including with the avifauna as this example makes clear. Canvasback is an authentic resident of North America and the Western Hemisphere. South Lakes Park is administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Source: "Canvasback," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, range map, photographs, description, resource links, accessed 2.7.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Canvasback/id

Sanderling (Calidris alba)

14 November 2009
North Jetty, San José Island
Port Aransas, Nueces County, Texas

This series of digital images (taken at Port Aransas, Texas) is dedicated to the memory of our friend, colleague and writer Carlos Guerra, whose invitation made our trip possible in November 2009. Carlos fished and spent time on the Texas Gulf Coast at Port Aransas throughout his life.
()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()()

These digital images were acquired both at the Fisherman's Wharf in Port Aransas, Texas, and at the North Jetty on San José Island (aka St. Jo Island in the local English parlance), famous for its fishing in the area. The series consists of nine images including eight aquatic birds and one saltwater fish: Sheepshead, Sanderling, Willet, Brown Pelican, Ruddy Turnstone, Great Blue Heron, Double-crested Cormorant, Laughing Gull and Snowy Egret. Here's the thumbnail sketch on the Sanderling at the All About Birds website: "The Sanderling’s black legs blur as it runs back and forth on the beach, picking or probing for tiny prey in the wet sand left by receding waves. Sanderlings are medium-sized “peep” sandpipers recognizable by their pale nonbreeding plumage, black legs and bill, and obsessive wave-chasing habits. Learn this species, and you’ll have an aid in sorting out less common shorebirds. This series of digital images (taken at Port Aransas, Texas) is dedicated to the memory of our friend, colleague and writer Carlos Guerra, whose invitation made our trip possible in November 2009. Carlos fished and spent time on the Texas Gulf Coast at Port Aransas throughout his life.

These digital images were acquired both at the Fisherman's Wharf in Port Aransas, Texas, and at the North Jetty on San José Island (aka St. Jo Island in the local English parlance), famous for its fishing in the area. The series consists of nine images including eight aquatic birds and one saltwater fish: Sheepshead, Sanderling, Willet, Brown Pelican, Ruddy Turnstone, Great Blue Heron, Double-crested Cormorant, Laughing Gull and Snowy Egret. Here's the thumbnail sketch on the Laughing Gull at the All About Birds website: "Swirling over beaches with strident calls and a distinctive, crisp black head, Laughing Gulls provide sights and sounds evocative of summer on the East Coast. You’ll run across this handsome gull in large numbers at beaches, docks, and parking lots, where they wait for handouts or fill the air with their raucous calls. Laughing Gulls are summer visitors to the Northeast and year-round sights on the coasts of the Southeast and the Gulf of Mexico.”

This was the only time the fantail would leave the dense understory of the shrubs. It can also be observed that this understory was the location of its nest. I believe only one fantail was observed, allowing me to assume that one sex hunts while the other is less active.The fantail was quite slow compared to the other birds I observed, and hopped from branch to branch more than it flew. Black-bellied Whistling Duck (Dendrocygna autumnalis)

9 April 2016
Centennial Park
Irving, Texas

We attended an event at the South Irving Public Library which is located next to the center of Centennial Park. Afterwards we walked the site and when leaving there was a small flock of four ducks flying over Delaware Creek (originally named Indian Run Creek by the first White settlers in the late 1840s) headed our way. We didn't know what kind of ducks these were but the last three pics we took on this date were of these ducks as they flew over the creek at a fast clip to our immediate left. Only when we had the chance to view the images (and admittedly the ISO needed to have been set faster on our camera to produce a better quality image), did we notice that these were Black-bellied Whistling Ducks. This is our first observation in the field of this duck in the North Texas region. These ducks have been extending their range northward in the United States. There's enough of the image present to make the ID possible. Thanks in advance.

Here's the thumbnail sketch from All About Birds for this duck: "The Black-bellied Whistling-Duck is a boisterous duck with a brilliant pink bill and an unusual, long-legged silhouette. In places like Texas and Louisiana, watch for noisy flocks of these gaudy ducks dropping into fields to forage on seeds, or loafing on golf course ponds. Listen for them, too—these ducks really do have a whistle for their call. Common south of the U.S., Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks occur in several southern states and are expanding northward." Black-bellied Whistling Duck is an authentic resident of North America and the Western Hemisphere. Centennial Park is administered by the City of Irving, Texas.

Source: "Black-bellied Whistling Duck," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, photographs, range map, description, resources, accessed 4.11.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck/id

The Tuli (Heteroscelus incanus) or Wandering Tattler can reach a height of 28 cm and is a rather nondescript, medium-sized wader with short legs. Its non-breeding plumage includes: dark slate-grey above, pale eyebrow in front of the eye, underparts are pale grey emerging to white on belly. In breeding plumage: the complete underparts have strong narrow black barring. The bill is long, straight and dark; the legs are yellowish green. They are fast and direct during flight with no wing bar. It has a diagnostic rippling trill of six to ten notes, gently accelerating but trailing off in volume; occasionally gives a variety of briefer calls.

Tuli feeds on small fish and aquatic invertebrates. They are common in coastal areas and it breeds mainly in Alaska then disperses throughout the central-southwest Pacific during the northern winter. 

Reference:
Watling, Dick and Kelly, Chloe Talbot. 2001. A Guide to the Birds of Fiji & Western Polynesia. Environmental Consultants (Fiji) Ltd. Fiji.

The Manuali'i (Porphyrio porphyrio) or Purple Swamphen is a large and beautiful bird is a dark purple, with a bright red beak that extends up over the forehead. This bird is more often heard than seen; it gives a loud screech with an echoing, honking quality. The Manuali'i prefers areas with thick undergrowth rather than true forest. It has a very wide diet, including many insects and much plant material. It sometimes gets into trouble with farmers because of its fondness for green bananas and taro tops. 

However, usually it does little damage, and repays it by eating soldier worms and other crop pests. In former times, the manuali'i was sometimes hunted, and this may be why it is so shy, usually running or flying off with loud screams as soon as it sees you. Like the ve'a, it nests in thick vegetation, either on the ground or in a low bush. It lays 3 or 4 eggs, and then the young leave the nest to follow their parents as soon as they hatch. It is even more widely distributed than the ve'a, occurring from southern Europe through Africa and all the way to Australia and New Zealand. It is much less common than the ve'a in American Samoa, but occurs in low numbers almost everywhere, especially in more remote plantation areas.

Reference:
Watling, Dick and Kelly, Chloe Talbot. 2001. A Guide to the Birds of Fiji & Western Polynesia. Environmental Consultants (Fiji) Ltd. Fiji.

Matuu or Reef Heron (Egretta sacra) can reach a height of 60 to 75 cm. They are found in in three distinct color phases in the Pacific west region. The white phase is pure white with yellow-green legs; the grey (or blue phase) is entirely slate-grey with a narrow white streak on the chin and throat; the mottled phase has a variable plumage, basically white with irregular and sometimes heavy, slate grey blotches. The beak is heavy; dark in grey phase birds and a dull yellow in white and mottled phase birds. They are slow and rather ponderous with the neck withdrawn with the feet projected just beyond the tail during flight. 
	
Matuu is generally silent, but sometimes utters a deep kraak, especially during courtship. These birds may be found in any aquatic habitat from an exposed reef to a small inland stream in thick forest. They feed on fish, crustaceans, mollusks, insects, and lizards. They build large untidy nests made of bare twigs and sticks on trees, cliff edges, under overhanging rocks, rock crevices in boulder screes, rock ledges in caves and occasionally on the ground on rocky islets. Nests usually contain two or four pale green eggs. The Matuu has a wide range from the eastern Indian Ocean through Southeast Asia, north to Japan and south to southern Australia, and New Zealand. It is uncommon in Niue but commonly found in the Pacific west region.

Reference:
Watling, Dick and Kelly, Chloe Talbot. 2001. A Guide to the Birds of Fiji & Western Polynesia. Environmental Consultants (Fiji) Ltd. Fiji.

Manusina or White tern (Gygis alba) can reach a height of 25 cm, and is a delicate pure white tern unlike any other species. The slender beak is black with a blue base and slightly upturned. The black eye has a black eye-ring and is distinctively prominent. The tail has a shallow fork with the wings appearing translucent from below during flight. It is characterized by its delicate, ethereal flight, fluttering erratically on its way. Manusina make a variety of noises that include: twanging, repeated quack, a purring crorr-r-r-rr, and a thin whistling note.

They are commonly seen over land when breeding or in adjacent coastal waters, but at other times forages well offshore and in pelagic waters. It feeds on small fish and squid, crustaceans, planktonic creatures, while deftly picking up food from the water surface or by plunge-diving. Manusina has a wide circum-equatorial range in the tropics and has been recorded as breeding in the Pacific west region.

Reference:
Watling, Dick and Kelly, Chloe Talbot. 2001. A Guide to the Birds of Fiji & Western Polynesia. Environmental Consultants (Fiji) Ltd. Fiji.

Eastern Kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus)

18 May 2016
Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge
Oklahoma State Highway 49
Indiahoma, Comanche County, Oklahoma

A single Eastern Kingbird was observed perched on a wire fence off to the side of Oklahoma State Highway 49 at the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge. A migratory bird, the Eastern Kingbird spends its year between North and South America. It winters in South America across a broad swath of the continent in a northwestern to central direction. According to All About Birds, while in South America Eastern Kingbird mostly feeds on fruit. It flies north to reproduce and spend its spring and summer and crosses the Caribbean and Central America while hugging the Gulf Coast of Mexico wending its way into Texas and the rest of the United States and Canada. Once there, it claims nearly the entire eastern two-thirds and most of the northwest of the United States and its Canadian territory extends from the Pacific Coast to the Atlantic. A truly transcontinental bird, Eastern Kingbird is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge is administered by the US Fish and Wildlife Service of the US Department of the Interior.

Source: "Eastern Kingbird," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, range map, photographs, description, resources, accessed 5.21.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Eastern_Kingbird/id

Cliff Swallow (Petrochelidon pyrrhonota)

15 June 2016
Elm Fork Park
Greenbelt Corridor Ray Roberts/Lewisville Lake FM 455 Access Area
Denton County, Texas

Cliff Swallow is a bird of the Americas, a transcontinental flier in the best sense of the word. It spends spring and summer raising its next generation from southern Mexico to western Alaska on the north. It literally flies over or spends parts of its life in almost every nation in the Western Hemisphere including the Caribbean, where it is a transient migrant flier. It winters in South America and is widely dispersed in the southern continent residing in all but one or two of the existing nations. Our observation caught Cliff Swallow still putting the finishing touches on its mud nest its labor nearly done. Here's the thumbnail sketch from All About Birds on Cliff Swallow: "Busy flocks of Cliff Swallows often swarm around bridges and overpasses in summer, offering passers-by a chance to admire avian architecture and family life at once. Clusters of their intricate mud nests cling to vertical walls, and when a Cliff Swallow is home you can see its bright forehead glowing from the dim entrance. These common, sociable swallows are nearly always found in large groups, whether they’re chasing insects high above the ground, preening on perches, or dipping into a river for a bath." Because of its hemispheric presence it goes without saying that Cliff Swallow is an authentic resident of this part of the world. Elm Fork Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

Source: "Cliff Swallow," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, range map, photographs, description, resources, accessed 6.15.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Cliff_Swallow/id

El zopilote negro,3 buitre negro americano, zopilote o jote de cabeza negra (Coragyps atratus) es la única especie del género Coragyps. Es un ave accipitriforme —aunque algunas clasificaciones lo incluyen en el orden Ciconiiformes—,4 y uno de los más abundantes miembros de la familia de los buitres del Nuevo Mundo (Cathartidae). Se extiende desde el sur de los Estados Unidos hasta el sur de Sudamérica.

A pesar de su apariencia y nombres similares, esta especie no tiene relación con el buitre negro eurasiático (Aegypius monachus). Esta última especie pertenece a la subfamilia de los buitres del Viejo Mundo (Aegypiinae), que es a su vez parte de la familia Accipitridae (la cual incluye a las águilas, halcones, milanos, gavilanes y aguiluchos), mientras que la especie americana es parte de la familia de los buitres del Nuevo Mundo (Cathartidae). Habita áreas relativamente abiertas que le proveen bosques aislados y tierras con arbustos.2 Tiene una envergadura de alas de 1,67 m, y un plumaje negro, cuello y cabeza grises y sin plumas, y un pico corto y en forma de gancho.

On this day, I only saw the one Bald Eagle. I heard a bunch of bird very upset and went to investigate. I saw the Eagle on the telephone pole eating a grey bird (possibly a dove). He used the top of the upright pole as a table, holding onto the bird with his talon and tearing at the bird. I got photos of him from two different angles.

This is a pair of Bald Eagles I had been seeing regularly, although they aren't always together. One is younger, with the head and tail feathers not fully white yet. The other is fully mature with fully white head and tail feathers. Often, I will be watching one for a short time and then the other will fly in. They often land on different telephone poles on either side of the Santa Ana River. On this day, they both landed on the same pole, which was handy for photographing them. 
They stayed for close to an hour before the older one flew away, very closely followed by the younger one. 
I've noticed that them pooping is a good sign they might be about to fly!

I saw this Bald Eagle mid-morning in the Santa Ana River. He was on a little sandy island, eating. I couldn't believe my eyes to see an Eagle here!! This was my first observation of an Eagle in the area. There were several Turkey Vultures waiting nearby. He finally walked off to the edge of the island and the vultures fought over what he left behind. I couldn't tell what he had been eating. I watched him for a long time and he finally flew away.

Wood Stork (Mycteria americana)

3 August 2016
Maverick County, Texas

These long shots were taken about 120-150 yards distant from the point where the birds were actually roosting. Wood Stork surprised us when we finally unpacked these images because we were expecting to find a roosting place for Great Egrets but instead found these vagrant Wood Storks, thirteen in all (which appear in part or whole) were counted based on the images obtained. These are likely first-year and older Wood Storks on their way between their nesting grounds and their eventual wintering grounds further south in Mexico, Central America or beyond. Apparently reports of Wood Storks nesting in Texas are next to none with but less than a handful of reports recorded of birds carrying sticks (presumably expressing nest-building behavior). Great Egrets shared the great tree and larger area where this particular roosting site is located, which is the usual behavior expressed by Wood Stork of keeping mixed company with other big birds. Wood Stork is not often seen in Maverick County but is not a stranger either apparently. Las Moras Creek in the northern part of the county from the Maverick/Kinney County line to the Río Bravo/Río Grande is often mentioned as a place where such observations have been made. In the United States, Wood Stork resides primarily along the shoreline from the Río Grande Valley north and east along the Gulf Coast to southern Florida. Vagrants are widely reported at points in between, according to the range map presented by NatureServe.  With its wide-ranging flight north and south in the Americas, Wood Stork is by all means an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Other day we saw an unusual small bird sitting on the fish trap buoy in front of my terrace. After consulting the bird guide I decided it was the Black Tern (Chlidonias niger). Unlike other birds hanging around the cove (cormorants and gulls), Teddy sat on the buoy for hours. Every so often it would fly around dipping toward the surface and (apparently) catching some fish. According to the bird guide, Black terns live around fresh waters when breeding, but can occur in coastal waters, estuaries and lagoons during flyover and in winter. It is middle of the August, and there were no big storms, so it is unclear how little juvenile tern landed in our little cove—probably separated from a migrating flock. The bird guide also notes that the Black terns are “highly sociable, both on breeding grounds and on passage.“ Our Teddy the Tern looked very out of place and lonely. After a day he had disappeared…

American White Pelican, Pelecanus erythrorhynchos. White plump body and wings, approximately 160-170 cm in length. The wings have a black tip, which weren't visible until the bird flew off. Bright orange webbed feet. The specimen's neck is nearly half the length of it's body, and its orange beak is of a similar size. Feathers cover the entire body apart from feet, legs, beak, and eyes. The specimen had a relatively short and square tail compared to its body.  The lack of a protrusion on the beak and duller colouration suggests the specimen is not in breeding season. Specimen appeared to be watching for fish to hunt along the Old Man River. The specimen did not move for nearly 10 minutes as it watched the water, save for its long neck.
